Ranked results

The table is sorted by p-value. FDR is the p-value corrected for the number of tests (Benjamini-Hochberg). A hit needs FDR below 5% and at least a 2-fold difference.

Why this matters

Two people with the same type of cancer can respond very differently to the same drug. Much of that difference traces back to changes in the tumor's DNA. Melanomas with a BRAF V600E mutation often shrink on BRAF inhibitors (Chapman 2011). Lung cancers with EGFR mutations respond to EGFR inhibitors (Lynch 2004). Breast cancers with extra copies of ERBB2, also called HER2, respond to drugs that block HER2 (Geyer 2006). Chronic myeloid leukemia, which is driven by the BCR-ABL fusion gene, responds to imatinib (Druker 2001). Doctors now test tumors for changes like these before choosing a treatment.

A gene change that predicts drug response is called a biomarker. This tool lets you test biomarker ideas against real data.

Where the evidence comes from

Cancer cell lines are one of the main places to look for links like these. A cell line is a population of tumor cells that keeps growing in the lab. The Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer project (GDSC), run by the Wellcome Sanger Institute with Massachusetts General Hospital, grew about 1,000 cancer cell lines, treated each one with hundreds of drugs at 5 or 9 doses for 72 hours, and measured how much each dose slowed growth. The team also recorded the mutations, copy-number changes and fusion genes in every line (Garnett 2012, Iorio 2016). The results are free for academic use.

How one result is made

The path from a dish of cells to a single yes-or-no answer on the Explorer page.

The problem this tool solves

Free data is not the same as easy data. The fitted results for this one release run to more than 200,000 rows. Drugs appear as ID numbers, the genetic data sits in a separate file, and about two thirds of the IC50 values lie beyond the highest dose tested, so they are estimates. Asking one simple question means merging files, filtering them, picking a statistical test and deciding what counts as a real difference. Each step is a chance for a silent mistake.

What the tool does

The Explorer answers one question at a time. Does this gene change alter how cancer cell lines respond to this drug, in this type of cancer? You choose the drug, the marker and the cancer type. The tool splits the tested lines into two groups, plots every line, runs the test and explains the result in plain language. It then checks the answer three more ways: across cancer types, in a second screen of the same drug when one exists, and with a second measure of response (AUC). The Scan page runs the same test for every drug or every marker at once and corrects for the number of tests.

Who it is for

Graduate students and instructors in cancer biology. A student can check whether a marker and drug idea holds up in real data before planning an experiment. An instructor can show a class what a biomarker result looks like, and what can go wrong with one.

What it cannot tell you

This is a teaching and research tool, not a clinical one. Cell lines grow on plastic without blood vessels, immune cells or neighboring tissue, and many have changed over decades in culture. A result here is a lead to test, not a prediction for a patient.

Results can also differ between screens. A 2013 comparison of two large cell line screens found poor agreement for many drugs (Haibe-Kains 2013). The Explorer shows a repeat-screen check whenever a drug was screened twice, and the Methods page lists every file and every step.

Known-answer checks

Marker and drug pairs where the answer was known before this tool existed. The tool runs each one live on the data below. A tool that failed these would not be trustworthy for new questions.
